newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Bomb, biggest protest raise tensions in Belgrade.
newsitem.headline: Bomb, biggest protest raise tensions in Belgrade.

text.p: Serbia's pro-democracy opposition used the Orthodox Christmas on Monday to stage its biggest protest yet, bringing hundreds of thousands of people onto the streets and paralysing much of central Belgrade.
Further heightening tensions, the Yugoslav United Left (JUL) party led by President Slobodan Milosevic's wife Mirjana Markovic said that a bomb was hurled at its headquarters in the city centre.

The JUL has been calling for a police crackdown on the Zajedno (Together) coalition, which has staged 50 consecutive days of massive protests after being denied recent election gains by what it says was fraud by the ruling Socialists.
Zajedno leaders denied involvement in the bombing and one said it had been staged.
"The disgraceful regime is resorting to its last desperate attempts to remain in power by staging some sort of bombing of JUL," said Vuk Draskovic.
There was a sign of cracks among the ruling party's own ranks in the form of a report that Belgrade Mayor Nabojsa Covic, a moderate, had submitted his resignation.
The sheer size of Monday's demonstrations was also a stark message to the authorities.

Unprecedented numbers of demonstrators converged on Republic Square and marched to St Sava's cathedral for midnight mass carrying traditional Yule logs, candles and torches. The Serbian Orthodox Church celebrates Christmas on January 7.
"We have never, never seen such a crowd in Belgrade," a traffic policeman.
Zajedno has been able to muster up to a quarter of million of people at protests but witnesses said this figures was definitely surpassed on Monday night.
Patriarch Pavle, who recently criticised Milosevic, set fire to a Yule log brought by marching students who had great difficulty getting through the crowd to the cathedral.
"This gathering is a Christmas uprising against stupidity, crime and tyranny," Draskovic said.
Police kept a low profile despite a ban on marches which Serbian Minister of the Interior Zoran Sokolovic refused to lift when he met a student delegation earlier in the day.
The students said they will stage a new form of protests on Wednesday under the slogan "No pardon for the cordon".
They say they will approach the police cordons and stay there until the police back off.
Belgraders brought their families and there was a festive atmosphere, with people blowing whistles and trumphets. Streets were packed for kilometres (miles) with demonstrators.

Sympathy for the opposition cause from General Momcilo Perisic, chief of the Yugoslav army general staff, was the latest crack in the 50-year monolith of leftist rule in federal Yugoslavia, now made up only of Serbia and tiny Montenegro.
Perisic told a student delegation that the army stayed out of politics but he favoured a democratic solution to the crisis that would help Yugoslavia rejoin Europe.
Seven weeks of protests have shaken Milosevic's authoritarian government and the West has warned him to democratise Yugoslavia or face international isolation.
Zajedno leader Zoran Djindjic revealed a new tactic to step up pressure on the government.

"We have decided to block the work of the state authorities -- on Tuesday and Wednesday you will get lists of all telephone numbers of all state institutions -- ministries, state TV and radio, Tanjug, and others,"
"Call them from dawn until dusk -- block their phones for 24 hours -- the less they work the less harm will be done to this country," he told a rally earlier in the evening.
An inquiry by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) has verified opposition claims to have won voting in 15 of Serbia's 18 largest cities, including Belgrade.

Serbia's Socialist government grudgingly admitted last week that Zajedno prevailed in a few of the smaller cities but insisted that in other districts no party gained a majority or the results were inconclusive and needed further study.
